about.title: About Timezone Converter
description: This timezone converter is meant for the practical work of comparing one local time against another without manually calculating offsets.

It is useful for scheduling calls, checking launch times, translating deadlines for distributed teams, and reviewing whether a UTC timestamp lines up with what people in a given city would actually see on the clock.

howTo.title: How to Use the Timezone Converter

steps.title: Choose the source timezone
steps.description: Start with the timezone where the original event time was created, not the timezone where you are currently sitting.

steps.title: Enter the local date and time
steps.description: Use the exact local time you want to compare, such as a meeting slot, release window, or customer deadline.

steps.title: Pick the destination timezone
steps.description: Select the city or timezone used by the other person, office, or system you need to coordinate with.

steps.title: Check the calendar date as well as the clock time
steps.description: Cross-timezone conversions often shift the day. Confirm whether the converted result lands earlier, later, or even on the next date.

tips: A meeting can fail even when the hour looks right if the converted date shifts to the previous or next day.
Daylight saving time changes are a common source of scheduling mistakes.
Use city-based timezone labels when possible so you do not mix up regions that currently share the same UTC offset.

features.title: Cross-region scheduling support
features.description: Useful for planning interviews, handoffs, launches, or customer calls across regions that do not share a working day.

features.title: DST-aware comparisons
features.description: The page is more useful than a static offset table because daylight saving rules can change the real-world answer.

features.title: City-oriented workflow
features.description: Thinking in cities helps avoid the common mistake of choosing the wrong offset label for the same region.

features.title: Date-shift visibility
features.description: The converted result helps you catch when a deadline lands on a different local calendar day for another team.

features.title: UTC translation help
features.description: Works well alongside timestamp checks when an event is stored in UTC but discussed in local business time.

features.title: Faster handoff planning
features.description: Useful for quickly seeing whether a proposed time fits overlap hours instead of forcing manual offset math.

faq.q: Why is timezone conversion harder than subtracting a fixed number of hours?
faq.a: Because real timezones are not just simple offsets. Daylight saving time, regional rules, and historical changes can all affect what the correct local time should be.

faq.q: What is the most common timezone mistake?
faq.a: People often convert the hour correctly but forget to check the date. A late-evening time in one region may already be the next morning somewhere else.

faq.q: Should I use UTC offsets or city names?
faq.a: City names are safer for most workflows because they track the timezone rules that actually apply to that location. A bare UTC offset can miss daylight saving changes.

faq.q: Can this help with meeting planning?
faq.a: Yes. It is especially useful when you need to compare one proposed time across multiple offices before sending an invite.

faq.q: Why does one timezone seem to change while another does not?
faq.a: Some regions observe daylight saving time and others do not. That means the gap between two cities can change during the year.

faq.q: Should I still verify important event times?
faq.a: Yes. For launches, contracts, travel, or other important events, confirm the final time in the system of record instead of relying on one conversion view alone.
